newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile boosts spy powers against "terrorist threat".
newsitem.headline: Chile boosts spy powers against "terrorist threat".

text.p: President Eduardo Frei on Monday announced wider spying powers for Chilean intelligence services and tighter prison security to prevent a repeat of last month's spectacular jailbreak by four leftist guerrillas.
Frei, saying new steps were needed "to face the terrorist threat," asked Congress to approve the measures, to be contained in a bill he plans to send to legislators this week.

If passed, the bill will let intelligence services recruit undercover agents and gain access to confidential bank records with a judge's permission, let police tap telephones and allow judges to bar guerrilla suspects from leaving the country.
Prison guards will get better weapons and jailed guerrillas will be separated and moved to various prisons throughout the country, said Frei.

Protective awnings are being built over outdoor recreation patios at jails and helicopters are now banned from flying over prisons -- measures aimed at preventing another air escape like that on Dec. 30, when four guerrillas fled a maximum security jail in a helicopter.

The guerrillas, convicted for a 1986 assassination attempt against then-military ruler Augusto Pinochet and the kidnapping of a newspaper magnate's son, were plucked from the jail's recreation area by a small helicopter.
"The country can rest asssured that all human and material resources are being deployed by the police to ... recapture the fugitives and fight against terrorism," said Frei in a speech.
Local newspaper reports have said security officials think some of the fugitives may have fled over the Andes into Argentina.

The jailbreak acutely embarrassed the government, which had long maintained Chile's guerrilla groups had been smashed. The head of the prison guard service resigned in disgrace and was replaced on Monday by former police general Mario Morales Mondaca.
Frei's rightist opponents have demanded the resignation of the interior, justice and defence ministers for negligence.

Much of the criticism echoed that against Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, who was accused of prematurely declaring victory in the anti-guerrilla war. On Dec. 17, Marxist rebels overran the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima taking high profile guests hostage.
Both episodes highlighted the resilience of South American left-wing guerrilla groups, most of them holdovers from the early 1980s, despite the region's return to civilian rule.
